title: Single-photon polarization tomography with an integrated metal-superconductor nanowire array
authors: Pierre Brosseau, Jiawei Wang, Giorgio Adamo, Anton N. Vetlugin, Cesare Soci
abstract: Light polarization is a primary degree of freedom for encoding quantum information. The scaling up of photonic quantum networks and computer architecture depends crucially on its precise characterization. This is typically achieved by placing external waveplates, polarizers, moving mounts, and recently metasurfaces, on top of the detectors. All these solutions complicate integration and scaling. Here we break convention with traditional architecture and present a monolithic, self-aligned metal-superconductor nanowire single photon detector (M-SNSPD) possessing intrinsic full polarization selectivity. Gold nanowires, co-fabricated atop NbTiN superconducting nanowires within the same lithographic footprint, act as polarization-selective plasmonic metamaterials inducing resonant absorption in the NbTiN. U-shaped wires provide linear polarization selectivity, while S-shaped meanders distinguish circular polarization, while retaining the high-count rates and low dark count rates of conventional SNSPDs. By arranging them into a four-pixel array we realize simultaneous projection onto four polarizations and demonstrate continuous polarization state tomography with an ensemble average fidelity exceeding 98%. Our approach opens new avenues towards scalable detector arrays with integrated plasmonic functionalities, for single photon polarimetry, imaging and spectroscopy.
summary: The paper presents a novel, monolithic metal-superconductor nanowire detector array that integrates polarization selectivity directly into the detector structure using plasmonic metamaterials. By arranging four specialized pixels, the device performs on-chip, high-fidelity quantum state tomography of single photons' polarization states. This breakthrough removes reliance on external optics, paving the way for scalable photonic quantum circuits.
main_problem: The scaling of photonic quantum networks requires precise, integrated characterization of single-photon polarization states without bulky external optics.
main_result: The developed monolithic detector array achieves intrinsic full polarization selectivity, enabling continuous polarization state tomography with an ensemble average fidelity exceeding 98%.
method: The authors fabricated a four-pixel metal-superconductor nanowire array where co-fabricated gold plasmonic metamaterials induce polarization-dependent resonant absorption in the superconducting nanowires.
model_or_system: The system is a monolithic, self-aligned M-SNSPD array containing U-shaped and S-shaped nanowires. These structures act as integrated polarizers by exploiting structural anisotropy (linear) and chirality (circular).
key_observables: Ensemble average fidelity (>98%), count rates following Malus's law, divergence in reflection spectra for different polarization components, and the reconstructed density matrix ($ho_{out}$).
important_parameters: High-count rate operation, low dark count rates, visibility ($V$), and the required complete basis set size (four pixels).
main_assumptions: The approach assumes that the gold overlayer acts as a hard etch mask for self-alignment, and minor deviations are attributed to fabrication imperfections.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the four-pixel array mapping to the Poincaré sphere; SEM images confirm polarization-dependent absorption mechanisms (U/S shapes); and theoretical plots show fidelity convergence limited by visibility ($V^{-2}$) and dimensionality constraints.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the need for integrated polarimetry, detailing the M-SNSPD design using plasmonics, demonstrating single-pixel polarization measurements (linear/circular), scaling up to a four-pixel array, and finally quantifying state tomography fidelity convergence across various input states.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses hardware limitations in quantum optics by integrating complex quantum measurement functionality (polarization analysis) onto the detector chip itself, which is crucial for building scalable photonic quantum processors.
